chunks: Routing differential pairs: layout guidelines. The question: How should it be routed? What are some layout guidelines that may differ from single-ended high-speed signals?
You route a differential pair as one object, not as two separate wires.
Both traces run side by side on the same layer, with the same spacing, the same length, the same vias and the same surroundings.
Anything that makes one trace see a different world than the other turns part of the signal into noise. The width and the gap together also set the pair's impedance.
Think of two dancers who must move in perfect mirror image. They stay the same distance apart, take the same number of steps and turn at the same moment.
If one has to walk around a table while the other goes straight, the mirror breaks. Pair routing is the same. Keep them together, and fix any difference right where it appears.
Pulling the pair closer requires narrower traces for the same 100 ohms.
Narrow traces have more conductor loss and are harder to fabricate consistently, which is why many designs choose moderate coupling ( s about w to 2w) rather than very tight.
Values come from the model behind the lab below; your fab's field solver gives the final numbers.
Differential impedance ( Z diff ): the impedance between the two traces, often 100 ohms (90 ohms for USB) ("Common characteristic impedance values").
Spacing: the gap between the two traces. Unlike single-ended routing, it helps set the impedance.
Intra-pair skew: the difference in arrival time between the two traces ("Differential pair skew: why it matters, how to fix").
Mode conversion: when imbalance turns some of the signal into common-mode noise.
Ground (return) vias: ground vias placed beside signal vias at layer changes so the return current can follow ("Vias in high-speed traces").
Say the board has 0. 2 mm of dielectric under the traces. A trace width of about 0. 24 mm with a 0. 2 mm gap gives roughly 100 ohms differential.
At a 90 degree bend the outer trace is longer by about (w plus s) pi over 2 equals 0. 44 times 1. 57 about 0. 69 mm, which is about 4 picoseconds.
So you add a small jog on the inner trace right after the bend. That is the whole idea.
"I route the two traces as one object: same layer, constant spacing set by the stackup for the target impedance, matched length, identical vias and symmetric bends, over a continuous reference plane.

The big differences from single-ended routing are that matching is within the pair and done locally at each bend or via, spacing sets the impedance, and there should be no stubs or one-sided obstacles.
Anything asymmetric converts differential signal into common-mode."
